Source: https://docs.rs/crate/nvml-wrapper/0.12.1

# nvml-wrapper

A safe and ergonomic Rust wrapper for the [NVIDIA Management Library](https://developer.nvidia.com/nvidia-management-library-nvml) (NVML),
a C-based programmatic interface for monitoring and managing various states within
NVIDIA GPUs.

```
use Nvml;
let nvml = init?;
// Get the first `Device` (GPU) in the system
let device = nvml.device_by_index?;
let brand = device.brand?; // GeForce on my system
let fan_speed = device.fan_speed?; // Currently 17% on my system
let power_limit = device.enforced_power_limit?; // 275k milliwatts on my system
let encoder_util = device.encoder_utilization?; // Currently 0 on my system; Not encoding anything
let memory_info = device.memory_info?; // Currently 1.63/6.37 GB used on my system
// ... and there's a whole lot more you can do. Most everything in NVML is wrapped and ready to go
```
*try the *

`basic_usage` example on your systemNVML is intended to be a platform for building 3rd-party applications, and is also the underlying library for NVIDIA's nvidia-smi tool.

## Usage

`nvml-wrapper` builds on top of generated bindings for NVML that make use of the
[ libloading](https://github.com/nagisa/rust_libloading) crate. This means the NVML library gets loaded upon
calling

`Nvml::init` and can return an error if NVML isn't present, making it
possible to drop NVIDIA-related features in your code at runtime on systems that
don't have relevant hardware.Successful execution of `Nvml::init` means:

- The NVML library was present on the system and able to be opened
- The function symbol to initialize NVML was loaded and called successfully
- An attempt has been made to load all other NVML function symbols

Every function you call thereafter will individually return an error if it couldn't
be loaded from the NVML library during the `Nvml::init` call.

Note that it's not advised to repeatedly call `Nvml::init` as the constructor
has to perform all the work of loading the function symbols from the library
each time it gets called. Instead, call `Nvml::init` once and store the resulting
`Nvml` instance somewhere to be accessed throughout the lifetime of your program
(perhaps in a [ once_cell](https://docs.rs/once_cell/latest/once_cell/sync/struct.Lazy.html)).

## NVML Support

This wrapper is being developed against and currently supports NVML version 12. Each new version of NVML is guaranteed to be backwards-compatible according to NVIDIA, so this wrapper should continue to work without issue regardless of NVML version bumps.

### Legacy Functions

Sometimes there will be function-level API version bumps in new NVML releases. For example:

```
nvmlDeviceGetComputeRunningProcesses
nvmlDeviceGetComputeRunningProcesses_v2
nvmlDeviceGetComputeRunningProcesses_v3
```
The older versions of the functions will generally continue to work with the newer NVML releases; however, the newer function versions will not work with older NVML installs.

By default this wrapper only provides access to the newest function versions.
Enable the `legacy-functions` feature if you require the ability to call older
functions.

## MSRV

The Minimum Supported Rust Version is currently 1.60.0. I will not go out of my way to avoid bumping this.

## Cargo Features

The `serde` feature can be toggled on in order to `#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]`
for every NVML data structure.

---

# nvml_wrapper - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/nvml-wrapper/0.12.1/target-redirect/nvml_wrapper/

## Expand description

A safe and ergonomic Rust wrapper for the [NVIDIA Management Library](https://developer.nvidia.com/nvidia-management-library-nvml) (NVML),
a C-based programmatic interface for monitoring and managing various states within
NVIDIA GPUs.

```
use nvml_wrapper::Nvml;
let nvml = Nvml::init()?;
// Get the first `Device` (GPU) in the system
let device = nvml.device_by_index(0)?;
let brand = device.brand()?; // GeForce on my system
let fan_speed = device.fan_speed(0)?; // Currently 17% on my system
let power_limit = device.enforced_power_limit()?; // 275k milliwatts on my system
let encoder_util = device.encoder_utilization()?; // Currently 0 on my system; Not encoding anything
let memory_info = device.memory_info()?; // Currently 1.63/6.37 GB used on my system
// ... and there's a whole lot more you can do. Most everything in NVML is wrapped and ready to go
```
NVML is intended to be a platform for building 3rd-party applications, and is also the underlying library for NVIDIA’s nvidia-smi tool.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

`nvml-wrapper` builds on top of generated bindings for NVML that make use of the
[ libloading](https://github.com/nagisa/rust_libloading) crate. This means the NVML library gets loaded upon
calling

`Nvml::init` and can return an error if NVML isn’t present, making it
possible to drop NVIDIA-related features in your code at runtime on systems that
don’t have relevant hardware.Successful execution of `Nvml::init` means:

- The NVML library was present on the system and able to be opened
- The function symbol to initialize NVML was loaded and called successfully
- An attempt has been made to load all other NVML function symbols

Every function you call thereafter will individually return an error if it couldn’t
be loaded from the NVML library during the `Nvml::init` call.

Note that it’s not advised to repeatedly call `Nvml::init` as the constructor
has to perform all the work of loading the function symbols from the library
each time it gets called. Instead, call `Nvml::init` once and store the resulting
`Nvml` instance somewhere to be accessed throughout the lifetime of your program
(perhaps in a [ once_cell](https://docs.rs/once_cell/latest/once_cell/sync/struct.Lazy.html)).

[§](https://docs.rs#nvml-support)NVML Support

This wrapper is being developed against and currently supports NVML version 11. Each new version of NVML is guaranteed to be backwards-compatible according to NVIDIA, so this wrapper should continue to work without issue regardless of NVML version bumps.

[§](https://docs.rs#legacy-functions)Legacy Functions

Sometimes there will be function-level API version bumps in new NVML releases. For example:

```
nvmlDeviceGetComputeRunningProcesses
nvmlDeviceGetComputeRunningProcesses_v2
nvmlDeviceGetComputeRunningProcesses_v3
```
The older versions of the functions will generally continue to work with the newer NVML releases; however, the newer function versions will not work with older NVML installs.

By default this wrapper only provides access to the newest function versions.
Enable the `legacy-functions` feature if you require the ability to call older
functions.

[§](https://docs.rs#msrv)MSRV

The Minimum Supported Rust Version is currently 1.51.0. I will not go out of my way to avoid bumping this.

[§](https://docs.rs#cargo-features)Cargo Features

The `serde` feature can be toggled on in order to `#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]`
for every NVML data structure.

# lib.rs - source

Source: https://docs.rs/nvml-wrapper/0.12.1/src/nvml_wrapper/lib.rs.html

# nvml_wrapper/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)/*!
[2](https://docs.rs#2)A safe and ergonomic Rust wrapper for the [NVIDIA Management Library][nvml] (NVML),
[3](https://docs.rs#3)a C-based programmatic interface for monitoring and managing various states within
[4](https://docs.rs#4)NVIDIA GPUs.
[5](https://docs.rs#5)
[6](https://docs.rs#6)```
[7](https://docs.rs#7)use nvml_wrapper::Nvml;
[8](https://docs.rs#8)# use nvml_wrapper::error::*;
[9](https://docs.rs#9)# fn test() -> Result<(), NvmlError> {
[10](https://docs.rs#10)
[11](https://docs.rs#11)let nvml = Nvml::init()?;
[12](https://docs.rs#12)// Get the first `Device` (GPU) in the system
[13](https://docs.rs#13)let device = nvml.device_by_index(0)?;
[14](https://docs.rs#14)
[15](https://docs.rs#15)let brand = device.brand()?; // GeForce on my system
[16](https://docs.rs#16)let fan_speed = device.fan_speed(0)?; // Currently 17% on my system
[17](https://docs.rs#17)let power_limit = device.enforced_power_limit()?; // 275k milliwatts on my system
[18](https://docs.rs#18)let encoder_util = device.encoder_utilization()?; // Currently 0 on my system; Not encoding anything
[19](https://docs.rs#19)let memory_info = device.memory_info()?; // Currently 1.63/6.37 GB used on my system
[20](https://docs.rs#20)
[21](https://docs.rs#21)// ... and there's a whole lot more you can do. Most everything in NVML is wrapped and ready to go
[22](https://docs.rs#22)# Ok(())
[23](https://docs.rs#23)# }
[24](https://docs.rs#24)```
[25](https://docs.rs#25)
[26](https://docs.rs#26)NVML is intended to be a platform for building 3rd-party applications, and is
[27](https://docs.rs#27)also the underlying library for NVIDIA's nvidia-smi tool.
[28](https://docs.rs#28)
[29](https://docs.rs#29)## Usage
[30](https://docs.rs#30)
[31](https://docs.rs#31)`nvml-wrapper` builds on top of generated bindings for NVML that make use of the
[32](https://docs.rs#32)[`libloading`][libloading] crate. This means the NVML library gets loaded upon
[33](https://docs.rs#33)calling `Nvml::init` and can return an error if NVML isn't present, making it
[34](https://docs.rs#34)possible to drop NVIDIA-related features in your code at runtime on systems that
[35](https://docs.rs#35)don't have relevant hardware.
[36](https://docs.rs#36)
[37](https://docs.rs#37)Successful execution of `Nvml::init` means:
[38](https://docs.rs#38)
[39](https://docs.rs#39)* The NVML library was present on the system and able to be opened
[40](https://docs.rs#40)* The function symbol to initialize NVML was loaded and called successfully
[41](https://docs.rs#41)* An attempt has been made to load all other NVML function symbols
[42](https://docs.rs#42)
[43](https://docs.rs#43)Every function you call thereafter will individually return an error if it couldn't
[44](https://docs.rs#44)be loaded from the NVML library during the `Nvml::init` call.
[45](https://docs.rs#45)
[46](https://docs.rs#46)Note that it's not advised to repeatedly call `Nvml::init` as the constructor
[47](https://docs.rs#47)has to perform all the work of loading the function symbols from the library
[48](https://docs.rs#48)each time it gets called. Instead, call `Nvml::init` once and store the resulting
[49](https://docs.rs#49)`Nvml` instance somewhere to be accessed throughout the lifetime of your program
[50](https://docs.rs#50)(perhaps in a [`once_cell`][once_cell]).
[51](https://docs.rs#51)
[52](https://docs.rs#52)## NVML Support
[53](https://docs.rs#53)
[54](https://docs.rs#54)This wrapper is being developed against and currently supports NVML version
[55](https://docs.rs#55)11. Each new version of NVML is guaranteed to be backwards-compatible according
[56](https://docs.rs#56)to NVIDIA, so this wrapper should continue to work without issue regardless of
[57](https://docs.rs#57)NVML version bumps.
[58](https://docs.rs#58)
[59](https://docs.rs#59)### Legacy Functions
[60](https://docs.rs#60)
[61](https://docs.rs#61)Sometimes there will be function-level API version bumps in new NVML releases.
[62](https://docs.rs#62)For example:
[63](https://docs.rs#63)
[64](https://docs.rs#64)```text
[65](https://docs.rs#65)nvmlDeviceGetComputeRunningProcesses
[66](https://docs.rs#66)nvmlDeviceGetComputeRunningProcesses_v2
[67](https://docs.rs#67)nvmlDeviceGetComputeRunningProcesses_v3
[68](https://docs.rs#68)```
[69](https://docs.rs#69)
[70](https://docs.rs#70)The older versions of the functions will generally continue to work with the
[71](https://docs.rs#71)newer NVML releases; however, the newer function versions will not work with
[72](https://docs.rs#72)older NVML installs.
[73](https://docs.rs#73)
[74](https://docs.rs#74)By default this wrapper only provides access to the newest function versions.
[75](https://docs.rs#75)Enable the `legacy-functions` feature if you require the ability to call older
[76](https://docs.rs#76)functions.
[77](https://docs.rs#77)
[78](https://docs.rs#78)## MSRV
[79](https://docs.rs#79)
[80](https://docs.rs#80)The Minimum Supported Rust Version is currently 1.51.0. I will not go out of my
[81](https://docs.rs#81)way to avoid bumping this.
[82](https://docs.rs#82)
[83](https://docs.rs#83)## Cargo Features
[84](https://docs.rs#84)
[85](https://docs.rs#85)The `serde` feature can be toggled on in order to `#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]`
[86](https://docs.rs#86)for every NVML data structure.
[87](https://docs.rs#87)
[88](https://docs.rs#88)[nvml]: https://developer.nvidia.com/nvidia-management-library-nvml
[89](https://docs.rs#89)[libloading]: https://github.com/nagisa/rust_libloading
[90](https://docs.rs#90)[once_cell]: https://docs.rs/once_cell/latest/once_cell/sync/struct.Lazy.html

[164](https://docs.rs#164)/// Determines the major version of the CUDA driver given the full version.
[165](https://docs.rs#165)///
[166](https://docs.rs#166)/// Obtain the full version via `Nvml.sys_cuda_driver_version()`.
[167](https://docs.rs#167)pub fn cuda_driver_version_major(version: i32) -> i32 {
[168](https://docs.rs#168)    version / 1000
[169](https://docs.rs#169)}
[170](https://docs.rs#170)
[171](https://docs.rs#171)/// Determines the minor version of the CUDA driver given the full version.
[172](https://docs.rs#172)///
[173](https://docs.rs#173)/// Obtain the full version via `NVML.sys_cuda_driver_version()`.
[174](https://docs.rs#174)pub fn cuda_driver_version_minor(version: i32) -> i32 {
[175](https://docs.rs#175)    (version % 1000) / 10
[176](https://docs.rs#176)}
[177](https://docs.rs#177)
[178](https://docs.rs#178)/**
[179](https://docs.rs#179)The main struct that this library revolves around.
[180](https://docs.rs#180)
[181](https://docs.rs#181)According to NVIDIA's documentation, "It is the user's responsibility to call `nvmlInit()`
[182](https://docs.rs#182)before calling any other methods, and `nvmlShutdown()` once NVML is no longer being used."
[183](https://docs.rs#183)This struct is used to enforce those rules.
[184](https://docs.rs#184)
[185](https://docs.rs#185)Also according to NVIDIA's documentation, "NVML is thread-safe so it is safe to make
[186](https://docs.rs#186)simultaneous NVML calls from multiple threads." In the Rust world, this translates to `NVML`
[187](https://docs.rs#187)being `Send` + `Sync`. You can `.clone()` an `Arc` wrapped `NVML` and enjoy using it on any thread.
[188](https://docs.rs#188)
[189](https://docs.rs#189)NOTE: If you care about possible errors returned from `nvmlShutdown()`, use the `.shutdown()`
[190](https://docs.rs#190)method on this struct. **The `Drop` implementation ignores errors.**
[191](https://docs.rs#191)
[192](https://docs.rs#192)When reading documentation on this struct and its members, remember that a lot of it,
[193](https://docs.rs#193)especially in regards to errors returned, is copied from NVIDIA's docs. While they can be found
[194](https://docs.rs#194)online [here](http://docs.nvidia.com/deploy/nvml-api/index.html), the hosted docs sometimes outdated
[195](https://docs.rs#195)and may not accurately reflect the version of NVML that this library is written for; beware. You
[196](https://docs.rs#196)should ideally read the doc comments on an up-to-date NVML API header. Such a header can be
[197](https://docs.rs#197)downloaded as part of the [CUDA toolkit](https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda-downloads).
[198](https://docs.rs#198)*/
[199](https://docs.rs#199)/// Describes which field ID numbering scheme the loaded NVML driver uses for
[200](https://docs.rs#200)/// IDs 251-273. NVIDIA broke ABI compatibility for these IDs between the
[201](https://docs.rs#201)/// original CUDA 13.0 release and CUDA 13.0 Update 1 (driver >= 580.82).
[202](https://docs.rs#202)///
[203](https://docs.rs#203)/// See <https://docs.nvidia.com/deploy/nvml-api/known-issues.html>
[204](https://docs.rs#204)#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
[205](https://docs.rs#205)pub enum FieldIdScheme {
[206](https://docs.rs#206)    /// Used by drivers before 580.82 (CUDA 12.x and original CUDA 13.0).
[207](https://docs.rs#207)    /// IDs 251-255 are CLOCKS_EVENT_REASON/POWER_SYNC, 256-273 are PWR_SMOOTHING.
[208](https://docs.rs#208)    V12,
[209](https://docs.rs#209)    /// Used by drivers >= 580.82 (CUDA 13.0 Update 1+).
[210](https://docs.rs#210)    /// IDs 251-268 are PWR_SMOOTHING, 269-273 are CLOCKS_EVENT_REASON/POWER_SYNC.
[211](https://docs.rs#211)    V13Update1,
[212](https://docs.rs#212)}
[213](https://docs.rs#213)
[214](https://docs.rs#214)pub struct Nvml {
[215](https://docs.rs#215)    lib: ManuallyDrop<NvmlLib>,
[216](https://docs.rs#216)    field_id_scheme: FieldIdScheme,
[217](https://docs.rs#217)}
[218](https://docs.rs#218)
[219](https://docs.rs#219)assert_impl_all!(Nvml: Send, Sync);
[220](https://docs.rs#220)
[221](https://docs.rs#221)impl std::fmt::Debug for Nvml {
[222](https://docs.rs#222)    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut std::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> std::fmt::Result {
[223](https://docs.rs#223)        f.write_str("NVML")
[224](https://docs.rs#224)    }
[225](https://docs.rs#225)}
[226](https://docs.rs#226)
[227](https://docs.rs#227)/// Parse a driver version string (e.g. "580.82.07") and determine the field ID scheme.
[228](https://docs.rs#228)/// Returns `V13Update1` for driver >= 580.82, `V12` otherwise.
[229](https://docs.rs#229)fn detect_field_id_scheme(driver_version: &str) -> FieldIdScheme {
[230](https://docs.rs#230)    let mut parts = driver_version.split('.');
[231](https://docs.rs#231)    let major: u32 = parts.next().and_then(|s| s.parse().ok()).unwrap_or(0);
[232](https://docs.rs#232)    let minor: u32 = parts.next().and_then(|s| s.parse().ok()).unwrap_or(0);
[233](https://docs.rs#233)
[234](https://docs.rs#234)    if major > 580 || (major == 580 && minor >= 82) {
[235](https://docs.rs#235)        FieldIdScheme::V13Update1
[236](https://docs.rs#236)    } else {
[237](https://docs.rs#237)        FieldIdScheme::V12
[238](https://docs.rs#238)    }
[239](https://docs.rs#239)}
[240](https://docs.rs#240)
[241](https://docs.rs#241)/// Translate a field ID from the canonical v12 numbering to the v13U1 numbering.
[242](https://docs.rs#242)/// Only affects IDs in the 251-273 range. IDs outside this range pass through unchanged.
[243](https://docs.rs#243)pub(crate) fn translate_field_id(scheme: FieldIdScheme, id: u32) -> u32 {
[244](https://docs.rs#244)    if scheme == FieldIdScheme::V12 {
[245](https://docs.rs#245)        return id;
[246](https://docs.rs#246)    }
[247](https://docs.rs#247)    // V13Update1 remapping:
[248](https://docs.rs#248)    //   v12 251-255 (CLOCKS_EVENT_REASON/POWER_SYNC) → v13U1 269-273
[249](https://docs.rs#249)    //   v12 256-273 (PWR_SMOOTHING) → v13U1 251-268
[250](https://docs.rs#250)    match id {
[251](https://docs.rs#251)        251..=255 => id + 18,
[252](https://docs.rs#252)        256..=273 => id - 5,
[253](https://docs.rs#253)        other => other,
[254](https://docs.rs#254)    }
[255](https://docs.rs#255)}
[256](https://docs.rs#256)
[257](https://docs.rs#257)impl Nvml {
[258](https://docs.rs#258)    /**
[259](https://docs.rs#259)    Handles NVML initialization and must be called before doing anything else.
[260](https://docs.rs#260)
[261](https://docs.rs#261)    While it is possible to initialize `NVML` multiple times (NVIDIA's docs state
[262](https://docs.rs#262)    that reference counting is used internally), you should strive to initialize
[263](https://docs.rs#263)    `NVML` once at the start of your program's execution; the constructors handle
[264](https://docs.rs#264)    dynamically loading function symbols from the `NVML` lib and are therefore
[265](https://docs.rs#265)    somewhat expensive.
[266](https://docs.rs#266)
[267](https://docs.rs#267)    Note that this will initialize NVML but not any GPUs. This means that NVML can
[268](https://docs.rs#268)    communicate with a GPU even when other GPUs in a system are bad or unstable.
[269](https://docs.rs#269)
[270](https://docs.rs#270)    By default, initialization looks for "libnvidia-ml.so" on linux and "nvml.dll"
[271](https://docs.rs#271)    on Windows. These default names should work for default installs on those
[272](https://docs.rs#272)    platforms; if further specification is required, use `Nvml::builder`.
[273](https://docs.rs#273)
[274](https://docs.rs#274)    # Errors
[275](https://docs.rs#275)
[276](https://docs.rs#276)    * `DriverNotLoaded`, if the NVIDIA driver is not running
[277](https://docs.rs#277)    * `NoPermission`, if NVML does not have permission to talk to the driver
[278](https://docs.rs#278)    * `Unknown`, on any unexpected error
[279](https://docs.rs#279)    */
[280](https://docs.rs#280)    // Checked against local
[281](https://docs.rs#281)    #[doc(alias = "nvmlInit_v2")]
[282](https://docs.rs#282)    pub fn init() -> Result<Self, NvmlError> {
[283](https://docs.rs#283)        Self::init_internal(LIB_PATH)
[284](https://docs.rs#284)    }
[285](https://docs.rs#285)
[286](https://docs.rs#286)    fn init_internal(path: impl AsRef<std::ffi::OsStr>) -> Result<Self, NvmlError> {
[287](https://docs.rs#287)        let lib = unsafe {
[288](https://docs.rs#288)            let lib = NvmlLib::new(path)?;
[289](https://docs.rs#289)            let sym = nvml_sym(lib.nvmlInit_v2.as_ref())?;
[290](https://docs.rs#290)
[291](https://docs.rs#291)            nvml_try(sym())?;
[292](https://docs.rs#292)            ManuallyDrop::new(lib)
[293](https://docs.rs#293)        };
[294](https://docs.rs#294)
[295](https://docs.rs#295)        let mut nvml = Self {
[296](https://docs.rs#296)            lib,
[297](https://docs.rs#297)            field_id_scheme: FieldIdScheme::V12,
[298](https://docs.rs#298)        };
[299](https://docs.rs#299)        nvml.field_id_scheme = nvml
[300](https://docs.rs#300)            .sys_driver_version()
[301](https://docs.rs#301)            .map(|v| detect_field_id_scheme(&v))
[302](https://docs.rs#302)            .unwrap_or(FieldIdScheme::V12);
[303](https://docs.rs#303)
[304](https://docs.rs#304)        Ok(nvml)
[305](https://docs.rs#305)    }
[306](https://docs.rs#306)
[307](https://docs.rs#307)    /**
[308](https://docs.rs#308)    An initialization function that allows you to pass flags to control certain behaviors.
[309](https://docs.rs#309)
[310](https://docs.rs#310)    This is the same as `init()` except for the addition of flags.
[311](https://docs.rs#311)
[312](https://docs.rs#312)    # Errors
[313](https://docs.rs#313)
[314](https://docs.rs#314)    * `DriverNotLoaded`, if the NVIDIA driver is not running
[315](https://docs.rs#315)    * `NoPermission`, if NVML does not have permission to talk to the driver
[316](https://docs.rs#316)    * `Unknown`, on any unexpected error
[317](https://docs.rs#317)
[318](https://docs.rs#318)    # Examples
[319](https://docs.rs#319)
[320](https://docs.rs#320)    ```
[321](https://docs.rs#321)    # use nvml_wrapper::Nvml;
[322](https://docs.rs#322)    # use nvml_wrapper::error::*;
[323](https://docs.rs#323)    use nvml_wrapper::bitmasks::InitFlags;
[324](https://docs.rs#324)
[325](https://docs.rs#325)    # fn main() -> Result<(), NvmlError> {
[326](https://docs.rs#326)    // Don't fail if the system doesn't have any NVIDIA GPUs
[327](https://docs.rs#327)    //
[328](https://docs.rs#328)    // Also, don't attach any GPUs during initialization
[329](https://docs.rs#329)    Nvml::init_with_flags(InitFlags::NO_GPUS | InitFlags::NO_ATTACH)?;
[330](https://docs.rs#330)    # Ok(())
[331](https://docs.rs#331)    # }
[332](https://docs.rs#332)    ```
[333](https://docs.rs#333)    */
[334](https://docs.rs#334)    #[doc(alias = "nvmlInitWithFlags")]
[335](https://docs.rs#335)    pub fn init_with_flags(flags: InitFlags) -> Result<Self, NvmlError> {
[336](https://docs.rs#336)        Self::init_with_flags_internal(LIB_PATH, flags)
[337](https://docs.rs#337)    }
[338](https://docs.rs#338)
[339](https://docs.rs#339)    fn init_with_flags_internal(
[340](https://docs.rs#340)        path: impl AsRef<std::ffi::OsStr>,
[341](https://docs.rs#341)        flags: InitFlags,
[342](https://docs.rs#342)    ) -> Result<Self, NvmlError> {
[343](https://docs.rs#343)        let lib = unsafe {
[344](https://docs.rs#344)            let lib = NvmlLib::new(path)?;
[345](https://docs.rs#345)            let sym = nvml_sym(lib.nvmlInitWithFlags.as_ref())?;
[346](https://docs.rs#346)
[347](https://docs.rs#347)            nvml_try(sym(flags.bits()))?;
[348](https://docs.rs#348)            ManuallyDrop::new(lib)
[349](https://docs.rs#349)        };
[350](https://docs.rs#350)
[351](https://docs.rs#351)        let mut nvml = Self {
[352](https://docs.rs#352)            lib,
[353](https://docs.rs#353)            field_id_scheme: FieldIdScheme::V12,
[354](https://docs.rs#354)        };
[355](https://docs.rs#355)        nvml.field_id_scheme = nvml
[356](https://docs.rs#356)            .sys_driver_version()
[357](https://docs.rs#357)            .map(|v| detect_field_id_scheme(&v))
[358](https://docs.rs#358)            .unwrap_or(FieldIdScheme::V12);
[359](https://docs.rs#359)
[360](https://docs.rs#360)        Ok(nvml)
[361](https://docs.rs#361)    }

[378](https://docs.rs#378)    /**
[379](https://docs.rs#379)    Use this to shutdown NVML and release allocated resources if you care about handling
[380](https://docs.rs#380)    potential errors (*the `Drop` implementation ignores errors!*).
[381](https://docs.rs#381)
[382](https://docs.rs#382)    # Errors
[383](https://docs.rs#383)
[384](https://docs.rs#384)    * `Uninitialized`, if the library has not been successfully initialized
[385](https://docs.rs#385)    * `Unknown`, on any unexpected error
[386](https://docs.rs#386)    */
[387](https://docs.rs#387)    // Thanks to `sorear` on IRC for suggesting this approach
[388](https://docs.rs#388)    // Checked against local
[389](https://docs.rs#389)    // Tested
[390](https://docs.rs#390)    #[doc(alias = "nvmlShutdown")]
[391](https://docs.rs#391)    pub fn shutdown(mut self) -> Result<(), NvmlError> {
[392](https://docs.rs#392)        let sym = nvml_sym(self.lib.nvmlShutdown.as_ref())?;
[393](https://docs.rs#393)
[394](https://docs.rs#394)        unsafe {
[395](https://docs.rs#395)            nvml_try(sym())?;
[396](https://docs.rs#396)        }
[397](https://docs.rs#397)
[398](https://docs.rs#398)        // SAFETY: we `mem::forget(self)` after this, so `self.lib` won't get
[399](https://docs.rs#399)        // touched by our `Drop` impl
[400](https://docs.rs#400)        let lib = unsafe { ManuallyDrop::take(&mut self.lib) };
[401](https://docs.rs#401)        mem::forget(self);
[402](https://docs.rs#402)
[403](https://docs.rs#403)        Ok(lib.__library.close()?)
[404](https://docs.rs#404)    }

[541](https://docs.rs#541)
[542](https://docs.rs#542)    /**
[543](https://docs.rs#543)    Acquire the handle for a particular device based on its index (starts at 0).
[544](https://docs.rs#544)
[545](https://docs.rs#545)    Usage of this function causes NVML to initialize the target GPU. Additional
[546](https://docs.rs#546)    GPUs may be initialized if the target GPU is an SLI slave.
[547](https://docs.rs#547)
[548](https://docs.rs#548)    You can determine valid indices by using `.device_count()`. This
[549](https://docs.rs#549)    function doesn't call that for you, but the actual C function to get
[550](https://docs.rs#550)    the device handle will return an error in the case of an invalid index.
[551](https://docs.rs#551)    This means that the `InvalidArg` error will be returned if you pass in
[552](https://docs.rs#552)    an invalid index.
[553](https://docs.rs#553)
[554](https://docs.rs#554)    NVIDIA's docs state that "The order in which NVML enumerates devices has
[555](https://docs.rs#555)    no guarantees of consistency between reboots. For that reason it is recommended
[556](https://docs.rs#556)    that devices be looked up by their PCI ids or UUID." In this library, that translates
[557](https://docs.rs#557)    into usage of `.device_by_uuid()` and `.device_by_pci_bus_id()`.
[558](https://docs.rs#558)
[559](https://docs.rs#559)    The NVML index may not correlate with other APIs such as the CUDA device index.
[560](https://docs.rs#560)
[561](https://docs.rs#561)    # Errors
[562](https://docs.rs#562)
[563](https://docs.rs#563)    * `Uninitialized`, if the library has not been successfully initialized
[564](https://docs.rs#564)    * `InvalidArg`, if index is invalid
[565](https://docs.rs#565)    * `InsufficientPower`, if any attached devices have improperly attached external power cables
[566](https://docs.rs#566)    * `NoPermission`, if the user doesn't have permission to talk to this device

[870](https://docs.rs#870)    /**
[871](https://docs.rs#871)    Gets the count of Host Interface Cards in the system.
[872](https://docs.rs#872)
[873](https://docs.rs#873)    # Errors
[874](https://docs.rs#874)
[875](https://docs.rs#875)    * `Uninitialized`, if the library has not been successfully initialized
[876](https://docs.rs#876)
[877](https://docs.rs#877)    # Device Support
[878](https://docs.rs#878)
[879](https://docs.rs#879)    Supports S-class products.
[880](https://docs.rs#880)    */
[881](https://docs.rs#881)    // Tested as part of the above method
[882](https://docs.rs#882)    #[doc(alias = "nvmlSystemGetHicVersion")]
[883](https://docs.rs#883)    pub fn hic_count(&self) -> Result<u32, NvmlError> {
[884](https://docs.rs#884)        let sym = nvml_sym(self.lib.nvmlSystemGetHicVersion.as_ref())?;
[885](https://docs.rs#885)
[886](https://docs.rs#886)        unsafe {
[887](https://docs.rs#887)            /*
[888](https://docs.rs#888)            NVIDIA doesn't even say that `count` will be set to the count if
[889](https://docs.rs#889)            `InsufficientSize` is returned. But we can assume sanity, right?
[890](https://docs.rs#890)
[891](https://docs.rs#891)            The idea here is:
[892](https://docs.rs#892)            If there are 0 HICs, NVML_SUCCESS is returned, `count` is set
[893](https://docs.rs#893)              to 0. We return count, all good.
[894](https://docs.rs#894)            If there is 1 HIC, NVML_SUCCESS is returned, `count` is set to
[895](https://docs.rs#895)              1. We return count, all good.
[896](https://docs.rs#896)            If there are >= 2 HICs, NVML_INSUFFICIENT_SIZE is returned.
[897](https://docs.rs#897)             `count` is theoretically set to the actual count, and we
[898](https://docs.rs#898)              return it.
[899](https://docs.rs#899)            */
[900](https://docs.rs#900)            let mut count: c_uint = 1;
[901](https://docs.rs#901)            let mut hics: [nvmlHwbcEntry_t; 1] = [mem::zeroed()];
[902](https://docs.rs#902)
[903](https://docs.rs#903)            match sym(&mut count, hics.as_mut_ptr()) {
[904](https://docs.rs#904)                nvmlReturn_enum_NVML_SUCCESS | nvmlReturn_enum_NVML_ERROR_INSUFFICIENT_SIZE => {
[905](https://docs.rs#905)                    Ok(count)
[906](https://docs.rs#906)                }
[907](https://docs.rs#907)                // We know that this will be an error
[908](https://docs.rs#908)                other => nvml_try(other).map(|_| 0),
[909](https://docs.rs#909)            }
[910](https://docs.rs#910)        }
[911](https://docs.rs#911)    }

[964](https://docs.rs#964)
[965](https://docs.rs#965)    /**
[966](https://docs.rs#966)    Request the OS and the NVIDIA kernel driver to rediscover a portion of the PCI
[967](https://docs.rs#967)    subsystem in search of GPUs that were previously removed.
[968](https://docs.rs#968)
[969](https://docs.rs#969)    The portion of the PCI tree can be narrowed by specifying a domain, bus, and
[970](https://docs.rs#970)    device in the passed-in `pci_info`. **If all of these fields are zeroes, the
[971](https://docs.rs#971)    entire PCI tree will be searched.** Note that for long-running NVML processes,
[972](https://docs.rs#972)    the enumeration of devices will change based on how many GPUs are discovered
[973](https://docs.rs#973)    and where they are inserted in bus order.
[974](https://docs.rs#974)
[975](https://docs.rs#975)    All newly discovered GPUs will be initialized and have their ECC scrubbed which
[976](https://docs.rs#976)    may take several seconds per GPU. **All device handles are no longer guaranteed
[977](https://docs.rs#977)    to be valid post discovery**. I am not sure if this means **all** device
[978](https://docs.rs#978)    handles, literally, or if NVIDIA is referring to handles that had previously
[979](https://docs.rs#979)    been obtained to devices that were then removed and have now been
[980](https://docs.rs#980)    re-discovered.
[981](https://docs.rs#981)
[982](https://docs.rs#982)    Must be run as administrator.
[983](https://docs.rs#983)
[984](https://docs.rs#984)    # Errors
[985](https://docs.rs#985)
[986](https://docs.rs#986)    * `Uninitialized`, if the library has not been successfully initialized
[987](https://docs.rs#987)    * `OperatingSystem`, if the operating system is denying this feature
[988](https://docs.rs#988)    * `NoPermission`, if the calling process has insufficient permissions to
[989](https://docs.rs#989)      perform this operation
[990](https://docs.rs#990)    * `NulError`, if an issue is encountered when trying to convert a Rust
[991](https://docs.rs#991)      `String` into a `CString`.
[992](https://docs.rs#992)    * `Unknown`, on any unexpected error
[993](https://docs.rs#993)
[994](https://docs.rs#994)    # Device Support
[995](https://docs.rs#995)
[996](https://docs.rs#996)    Supports Pascal and newer fully supported devices.
[997](https://docs.rs#997)
[998](https://docs.rs#998)    Some Kepler devices are also supported (that's all NVIDIA says, no specifics).
[999](https://docs.rs#999)
[1000](https://docs.rs#1000)    # Platform Support
[1001](https://docs.rs#1001)
[1002](https://docs.rs#1002)    Only supports Linux.
[1003](https://docs.rs#1003)    */

# Device in nvml_wrapper::device - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/nvml-wrapper/0.12.1/nvml_wrapper/device/struct.Device.html

`pub struct Device<'nvml> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Struct that represents a device on the system.

Obtain a `Device` with the various methods available to you on the `Nvml`
struct.

Lifetimes are used to enforce that each `Device` instance cannot be used after
the `Nvml` instance it was obtained from is dropped:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use nvml_wrapper::Nvml;
let nvml = Nvml::init()?;
let device = nvml.device_by_index(0)?;
drop(nvml);
// This won't compile
device.fan_speed(0)?;
```
This means you shouldn’t have to worry about calls to `Device` methods returning
`Uninitialized` errors.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Gets the current and default state of auto boosted clocks.

Auto boosted clocks are enabled by default on some hardware, allowing the GPU to run as fast as thermals will allow it to.

On Pascal and newer hardware, auto boosted clocks are controlled through application
clocks. Use `.set_applications_clocks()` and `.reset_applications_clocks()` to control
auto boost behavior.

- `GpuLost`, if this- `Device`has fallen off the bus or is otherwise inaccessible
- `UnexpectedVariant`, for which you can read the docs for
- `Unknown`, on any unexpected error

[§](https://docs.rs#device-support-3)Device Support

BAR1 memory is used to map the FB (device memory) so that it can be directly accessed by the CPU or by 3rd party devices (peer-to-peer on the PCIe bus).

#### pub fn [memory_affinity](https://docs.rs#method.memory_affinity)(
    &self,
    size: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html),
    scope: [nvmlAffinityScope_t](https://docs.rs/nvml-wrapper-sys/0.9.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/nvml_wrapper_sys/bindings/type.nvmlAffinityScope_t.html),
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[c_ulong](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/os/raw/type.c_ulong.html)>, [NvmlError](https://docs.rs/error/enum.NvmlError.html)>

Gets the NUMA nodes physically close to the GPU.

Main goal is to facilitate memory placement optimisations for multi CPU/GPU settings.
Node (set) size needs to be something like `<Number of nodes> / (std::mem::size_of::<c_ulong>() / 8) + 1`

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-5)Errors

- `Uninitialized`, if the library has not been successfully initialized
- `InvalidArg`, if this- `Device`is invalid
- `NotSupported`, if this- `Device`does not support this query
- `GpuLost`, if this- `Device`has fallen off the bus or is otherwise inaccessible
- `Unknown`, on any unexpected error

Gets the board ID for this `Device`, from 0-N.

Devices with the same boardID indicate GPUs connected to the same PLX. Use in
conjunction with `.is_multi_gpu_board()` to determine if they are on the same
board as well.

The boardID returned is a unique ID for the current config. Uniqueness and ordering across reboots and system configs is not guaranteed (i.e if a Tesla K40c returns 0x100 and the two GPUs on a Tesla K10 in the same system return 0x200, it is not guaranteed that they will always return those values. They will, however, always be different from each other).

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-17)Errors

- `Uninitialized`, if the library has not been successfully initialized
- `InvalidArg`, if this- `Device`is invalid
- `GpuLost`, if this- `Device`has fallen off the bus or is otherwise inaccessible
- `Unknown`, on any unexpected error

Gets a vector of bitmasks with the ideal CPU affinity for this `Device`.

The results are sized to `size`. For example, if processors 0, 1, 32, and 33 are
ideal for this `Device` and `size` == 2, result[0] = 0x3, result[1] = 0x3.

64 CPUs per unsigned long on 64-bit machines, 32 on 32-bit machines.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/nvml_wrapper/device.rs.html#1088-1118)

#### pub fn [confidential_compute_gpu_attestation_report](https://docs.rs#method.confidential_compute_gpu_attestation_report)(
    &self,
    nonce: [[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html); [32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.array.html)],
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[ConfidentialComputeGpuAttestationReport](https://docs.rs/structs/device/struct.ConfidentialComputeGpuAttestationReport.html), [NvmlError](https://docs.rs/error/enum.NvmlError.html)>

Fetches the confidential compute attestation report for this [ Device](https://docs.rs/struct.Device.html).

This method retrieves a comprehensive attestation report from the device, which includes:

- A 32-byte nonce
- The attestation report size (as big-endian bytes)
- The attestation report data (up to 8192 bytes)
- A flag indicating if CEC attestation is present (as big-endian bytes)
- The CEC attestation report size (as big-endian bytes)
- The CEC attestation report data (up to 4096 bytes)

The returned vector contains all these components concatenated together in the order listed above.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-26)Errors

- `Uninitialized`, if the library has not been successfully initialized
- `InvalidArg`, if device is invalid or memory is NULL
- `NotSupported`, if this query is not supported by the device
- `Unknown`, on any unexpected error

Utilization stats are returned for processes that had a non-zero utilization stat

a timestamp retrieved from a previous query will target samples taken since that
timestamp.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/nvml_wrapper/device.rs.html#2689-2701)#### pub fn [memory_info](https://docs.rs#method.memory_info)(&self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[MemoryInfo](https://docs.rs/struct_wrappers/device/struct.MemoryInfo.html), [NvmlError](https://docs.rs/error/enum.NvmlError.html)>

#### pub fn [memory_info](https://docs.rs#method.memory_info)(&self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[MemoryInfo](https://docs.rs/struct_wrappers/device/struct.MemoryInfo.html), [NvmlError](https://docs.rs/error/enum.NvmlError.html)>

Gets the amount of used, free and total memory available on this `Device`, in bytes.

Note that enabling ECC reduces the amount of total available memory due to the extra required parity bits.

Also note that on Windows, most device memory is allocated and managed on startup by Windows.

Under Linux and Windows TCC (no physical display connected), the reported amount
of used memory is equal to the sum of memory allocated by all active channels on
this `Device`.

[§](https://docs.rs#device-support-47)Device Support

Supports Ampere and newer fully supported devices.

Checks if the `Device`supports multi partitioned GPU feature and if enabled.
Not to confuse with `is_multi_gpu_board`, MIG is a single GPU
being able to be split into isolated instances, a sort of “NUMA” for GPU.
If the `Device` supports MIG, we can have its current mode (enabled/disabled)
and, if set, its pending mode for the next system reboot.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/nvml_wrapper/device.rs.html#3555-3591)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/nvml_wrapper/device.rs.html#3555-3591)

Gets recent samples for this `Device`.

`last_seen_timestamp` represents the CPU timestamp in μs. Passing in `None`
will fetch all samples maintained in the underlying buffer; you can
alternatively pass in a timestamp retrieved from the date of the previous
query in order to obtain more recent samples.

The advantage of using this method for samples in contrast to polling via existing methods is to get higher frequency data at a lower polling cost.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-92)Errors

- `Uninitialized`, if the library has not been successfully initialized
- `InvalidArg`, if this- `Device`is invalid
- `NotSupported`, if this query is not supported by this- `Device`
- `GpuLost`, if this- `Device`has fallen off the bus or is otherwise inaccessible
- `NotFound`, if sample entries are not found
- `UnexpectedVariant`, check that error’s docs for more info
- `Unknown`, on any unexpected error

[§](https://docs.rs#device-support-58)Device Support

Supports Kepler and newer fully supported devices.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use nvml_wrapper::enum_wrappers::device::Sampling;
// Passing `None` indicates that we want all `Power` samples in the sample buffer
let power_samples = device.samples(Sampling::Power, None)?;
// Take the first sample from the vector, if it exists...
if let Some(sample) = power_samples.get(0) {
    // ...and now we can get all `ProcessorClock` samples that exist with a later
    // timestamp than the `Power` sample.
    let newer_clock_samples = device.samples(Sampling::ProcessorClock, sample.timestamp)?;
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/nvml_wrapper/device.rs.html#3644-3672)#### pub fn [field_values_for](https://docs.rs#method.field_values_for)(
    &self,
    id_slice: &[[FieldId](https://docs.rs/structs/device/struct.FieldId.html)],
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[FieldValueSample](https://docs.rs/struct_wrappers/device/struct.FieldValueSample.html), [NvmlError](https://docs.rs/error/enum.NvmlError.html)>>, [NvmlError](https://docs.rs/error/enum.NvmlError.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/nvml_wrapper/device.rs.html#3644-3672)

#### pub fn [field_values_for](https://docs.rs#method.field_values_for)(
    &self,
    id_slice: &[[FieldId](https://docs.rs/structs/device/struct.FieldId.html)],
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[FieldValueSample](https://docs.rs/struct_wrappers/device/struct.FieldValueSample.html), [NvmlError](https://docs.rs/error/enum.NvmlError.html)>>, [NvmlError](https://docs.rs/error/enum.NvmlError.html)>

Get values for the given slice of `FieldId`s.

NVIDIA’s docs say that if any of the `FieldId`s are populated by the same driver
call, the samples for those IDs will be populated by a single call instead of
a call per ID. It would appear, then, that this is essentially a “batch-request”
API path for better performance.

There are too many field ID constants defined in the header to reasonably
wrap them with an enum in this crate. Instead, I’ve re-exported the defined
ID constants at `nvml_wrapper::sys_exports::field_id::*`; stick those
constants in `FieldId`s for use with this function.

- `InvalidArg`, if- `id_slice`has a length of zero

[§](https://docs.rs#inner-result)Inner `Result`

- `UnexpectedVariant`, check that error’s docs for more info

Gets the total ECC error counts for this `Device`.

Only applicable to devices with ECC. The total error count is the sum of errors across each of the separate memory systems, i.e. the total set of errors across the entire device.

[§](https://docs.rs#device-support-69)Device Support

Supports Fermi and newer fully supported devices. Requires `InfoRom::ECC` version 1.0
or higher. Requires ECC mode to be enabled.

Gets the globally unique immutable UUID associated with this `Device` as a 5 part
hexadecimal string.

This UUID augments the immutable, board serial identifier. It is a globally unique
identifier and is the *only* available identifier for pre-Fermi-architecture products.
It does NOT correspond to any identifier printed on the board.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-108)Errors

- `Uninitialized`, if the library has not been successfully initialized
- `InvalidArg`, if this- `Device`is invalid
- `NotSupported`, if this- `Device`does not support this feature
- `GpuLost`, if this- `Device`has fallen off the bus or is otherwise inaccessible
- `Utf8Error`, if the string obtained from the C function is not valid Utf8
- `Unknown`, on any unexpected error

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

The UUID can be used to compare two `Device`s and find out if they represent
the same physical device:

```
if device1.uuid()? == device2.uuid()? {
    println!("`device1` represents the same physical device that `device2` does.");
}
```

Gets the duration of time during which this `Device` was throttled (lower than the
requested clocks) due to power or thermal constraints.

This is important to users who are trying to understand if their GPUs throttle at any point while running applications. The difference in violation times at two different reference times gives the indication of a GPU throttling event.

Violation for thermal capping is not supported at this time.

Gets the current PCIe link speed for this [ Device](https://docs.rs/struct.Device.html).

NVML docs say the returned value is in “MBPS”. Looking at the output of
this function, however, seems to imply it actually returns the transfer
rate per lane of the PCIe link in MT/s, not the combined multi-lane
throughput. See [ PcieLinkMaxSpeed](https://docs.rs/enums/device/enum.PcieLinkMaxSpeed.html) for the same discussion.

For example, on my machine currently:

Right now the device is connected via a PCIe gen 4 x16 interface and

`pcie_link_speed()`returns 16000

This lines up with the “transfer rate per lane numbers” listed at
[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PCI_Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PCI_Express). PCIe gen 4 provides 16.0 GT/s.
Also, checking my machine at a different moment yields:

Right now the device is connected via a PCIe gen 2 x16 interface and

`pcie_link_speed()`returns 5000

Which again lines up with the table on the page above; PCIe gen 2 provides 5.0 GT/s.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/nvml_wrapper/device.rs.html#4696-4700)#### pub fn [reset_applications_clocks](https://docs.rs#method.reset_applications_clocks)(&mut self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html), [NvmlError](https://docs.rs/error/enum.NvmlError.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/nvml_wrapper/device.rs.html#4696-4700)

#### pub fn [reset_applications_clocks](https://docs.rs#method.reset_applications_clocks)(&mut self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html), [NvmlError](https://docs.rs/error/enum.NvmlError.html)>

Resets the application clock to the default value.

This is the applications clock that will be used after a system reboot or a driver
reload. The default value is a constant, but the current value be changed with
`.set_applications_clocks()`.

On Pascal and newer hardware, if clocks were previously locked with
`.set_applications_clocks()`, this call will unlock clocks. This returns clocks
to their default behavior of automatically boosting above base clocks as
thermal limits allow.

- `Unknown`, on any unexpected error

[§](https://docs.rs#device-support-72)Device Support

Supports Fermi and newer non-GeForce fully supported devices and Maxwell or newer GeForce devices.

Try to set the current state of auto boosted clocks on this `Device`.

Auto boosted clocks are enabled by default on some hardware, allowing the GPU to run as fast as thermals will allow it to. Auto boosted clocks should be disabled if fixed clock rates are desired.

On Pascal and newer hardware, auto boosted clocks are controlled through application
clocks. Use `.set_applications_clocks()` and `.reset_applications_clocks()` to control
auto boost behavior.

Non-root users may use this API by default, but access can be restricted by root using
`.set_api_restriction()`.

Note: persistence mode is required to modify the curent auto boost settings and therefore must be enabled.

Accounting stats capture GPU utilization and other statistics across the lifetime
of a process. Accounting stats can be queried during the lifetime of the process
and after its termination. The `time` field in `AccountingStats` is reported as
zero during the lifetime of the process and updated to the actual running time
after its termination.

Accounting stats are kept in a circular buffer; newly created processes overwrite information regarding old processes.

Note:

- Accounting mode needs to be on. See `.is_accounting_enabled()`.
- Only compute and graphics applications stats can be queried. Monitoring applications can’t be queried since they don’t contribute to GPU utilization.
- If a PID collision occurs, the stats of the latest process (the one that terminated last) will be reported.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-132)Errors

- `Uninitialized`, if the library has not been successfully initialized
- `InvalidArg`, if the- `Device`is invalid
- `NotFound`, if the process stats were not found
- `NotSupported`, if this- `Device`does not support this feature or accounting mode is disabled
- `Unknown`, on any unexpected error

[§](https://docs.rs#device-support-81)Device Support

Suports Kepler and newer fully supported devices.

[§](https://docs.rs#warning)Warning

On Kepler devices, per-process stats are accurate *only if* there’s one process
running on this `Device`.

Enables or disables per-process accounting.

Requires root/admin permissions.

Note:

- This setting is not persistent and will default to disabled after the driver unloads. Enable persistence mode to be sure the setting doesn’t switch off to disabled.
- Enabling accounting mode has no negative impact on GPU performance.
- Disabling accounting clears accounting information for all PIDs

- `InvalidArg`, if the- `Device`is invalid

- `NoPermission`, if the user doesn’t have permission to perform this operation
- `Unknown`, on any unexpected error

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/nvml_wrapper/device.rs.html#5236-5244)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/nvml_wrapper/device.rs.html#5236-5244)

Sets clocks that applications will lock to.

Sets the clocks that compute and graphics applications will be running at. e.g. CUDA driver requests these clocks during context creation which means this property defines clocks at which CUDA applications will be running unless some overspec event occurs (e.g. over power, over thermal or external HW brake).

Can be used as a setting to request constant performance. Requires root/admin permissions.

On Pascal and newer hardware, this will automatically disable automatic boosting
of clocks. On K80 and newer Kepler and Maxwell GPUs, users desiring fixed performance
should also call `.set_auto_boosted_clocks(false)` to prevent clocks from automatically
boosting above the clock value being set here.

You can determine valid `mem_clock` and `graphics_clock` arg values via
[ Self::supported_memory_clocks()](https://docs.rs/struct.Device.html#method.supported_memory_clocks) and

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Device.html#method.supported_graphics_clocks)

`Self::supported_graphics_clocks()`Note that after a system reboot or driver reload applications clocks go back to their default value.

See also [ Self::set_mem_locked_clocks()](https://docs.rs/struct.Device.html#method.set_mem_locked_clocks).

- `Unknown`, on any unexpected error

[§](https://docs.rs#device-support-91)Device Support

Supports GK110 M-class and X-class Tesla products from the Kepler family. Modes
`LowDP` and `AllOn` are supported on fully supported GeForce products. Not
supported on Quadro and Tesla C-class products.

Sets the persistence mode for this `Device`.

The persistence mode determines whether the GPU driver software is torn down after the last client exits.

This operation takes effect immediately and requires root/admin permissions. It is not persistent across reboots; after each reboot it will default to disabled.

Note that after disabling persistence on a device that has its own NUMA
memory, this `Device` handle will no longer be valid, and to continue to
interact with the physical device that it represents you will need to
obtain a new `Device` using the methods available on the `Nvml` struct.
This limitation is currently only applicable to devices that have a
coherent NVLink connection to system memory.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/nvml_wrapper/device.rs.html#5837-5872)#### pub fn [register_events](https://docs.rs#method.register_events)(
    &self,

) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[EventSet](https://docs.rs/event/struct.EventSet.html)<'nvml>, [NvmlErrorWithSource](https://docs.rs/error/struct.NvmlErrorWithSource.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/nvml_wrapper/device.rs.html#5837-5872)

#### pub fn [register_events](https://docs.rs#method.register_events)(
    &self,
    events: [EventTypes](https://docs.rs/bitmasks/event/struct.EventTypes.html),
    set: [EventSet](https://docs.rs/event/struct.EventSet.html)<'nvml>,
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[EventSet](https://docs.rs/event/struct.EventSet.html)<'nvml>, [NvmlErrorWithSource](https://docs.rs/error/struct.NvmlErrorWithSource.html)>

Starts recording the given `EventTypes` for this `Device` and adding them
to the specified `EventSet`.

Use `.supported_event_types()` to find out which events you can register for
this `Device`.

**Unfortunately, due to the way  error-chain works, there is no way to
return the set if it is still valid after an error has occurred with the
register call.** The set that you passed in will be freed if any error
occurs and will not be returned to you. This is not desired behavior
and I will fix it as soon as it is possible to do so.

All events that occurred before this call was made will not be recorded.

ECC events are only available on `Device`s with ECC enabled. Power capping events
are only available on `Device`s with power management enabled.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-149)Errors

- `Uninitialized`, if the library has not been successfully initialized
- `InvalidArg`, if- `events`is invalid (shouldn’t occur?)
- `NotSupported`, if the platform does not support this feature or some of the requested event types.
- `GpuLost`, if this- `Device`has fallen off the bus or is otherwise inaccessible
- `Unknown`, on any unexpected error.- **If this error is returned, the**. NVIDIA’s docs say that this error means that the set is in an invalid state.- `set`you passed in has had its resources freed and will not be returned to you

[§](https://docs.rs#device-support-95)Device Support

Supports Fermi and newer fully supported devices.

[§](https://docs.rs#platform-support-11)Platform Support

Only supports Linux.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-2)Examples

```
use nvml_wrapper::bitmasks::event::EventTypes;
let set = nvml.create_event_set()?;
/*
Register both `CLOCK_CHANGE` and `PSTATE_CHANGE`.
`let set = ...` is a quick way to re-bind the set to the same variable, since
`.register_events()` consumes the set in order to enforce safety and returns it
if everything went well. It does *not* require `set` to be mutable as nothing
is being mutated.
*/
let set = device.register_events(
    EventTypes::CLOCK_CHANGE |
    EventTypes::PSTATE_CHANGE,
    set
)?;
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/nvml_wrapper/device.rs.html#6384-6441)#### pub fn [remove](https://docs.rs#method.remove)<T: [Into](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.Into.html)<[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[PciInfo](https://docs.rs/struct_wrappers/device/struct.PciInfo.html)>>>(

#### pub fn [remove](https://docs.rs#method.remove)<T: [Into](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.Into.html)<[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[PciInfo](https://docs.rs/struct_wrappers/device/struct.PciInfo.html)>>>(
    self,
    pci_info: T,
    gpu_state: [DetachGpuState](https://docs.rs/enum_wrappers/device/enum.DetachGpuState.html),
    link_state: [PcieLinkState](https://docs.rs/enum_wrappers/device/enum.PcieLinkState.html),
) -> ([Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html), [NvmlErrorWithSource](https://docs.rs/error/struct.NvmlErrorWithSource.html)>, [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[Device](https://docs.rs/struct.Device.html)<'nvml>>)

Removes this `Device` from the view of both NVML and the NVIDIA kernel driver.

If you pass `None` as `pci_info`, `.pci_info()` will be called in order to obtain
`PciInfo` to be used within this method.

This call only works if no other processes are attached. If other processes
are attached when this is called, the `InUse` error will be returned and
this `Device` will return to its original draining state. The only situation
where this can occur is if a process was and is still using this `Device`
before the call to `set_drain()` was made and it was enabled. Note that
persistence mode counts as an attachment to this `Device` and thus must be
disabled prior to this call.

For long-running NVML processes, please note that this will change the enumeration of current GPUs. As an example, if there are four GPUs present and the first is removed, the new enumeration will be 0-2. Device handles for the removed GPU will be invalid.

NVIDIA doesn’t provide much documentation about the `gpu_state` and `link_state`
parameters, so you’re on your own there. It does say that the `gpu_state`
controls whether or not this `Device` should be removed from the kernel.

Must be run as administrator.

[§](https://docs.rs#bad-ergonomics-explanation)Bad Ergonomics Explanation

Previously the design of `error-chain` made it impossible to return stuff
with generic lifetime parameters. The crate’s errors are now based on
`std::error::Error`, so this situation no longer needs to be, but I haven’t
made time to re-work it.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-159)Errors

- `Uninitialized`, if the library has not been successfully initialized
- `NotSupported`, if this- `Device`doesn’t support this feature
- `GpuLost`, if this- `Device`has fallen off the bus or is otherwise inaccessible
- `InUse`, if this- `Device`is still in use and cannot be removed

In addition, all of the errors returned by:

- `.pci_info()`
- `PciInfo.try_into()`

[§](https://docs.rs#device-support-101)Device Support

Supports Pascal and newer fully supported devices.

Some Kepler devices are also supported (that’s all NVIDIA says, no specifics).

[§](https://docs.rs#platform-support-20)Platform Support

Only supports Linux.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-6)Examples

How to handle error case:

```
match device.remove(None, DetachGpuState::Remove, PcieLinkState::ShutDown) {
    (Ok(()), None) => println!("Successful call, `Device` removed"),
    (Err(e), Some(d)) => println!("Unsuccessful call. `Device`: {:?}", d),
    _ => println!("Something else",)
}
```
Demonstration of the `pci_info` parameter’s use:

```
// Pass `None`, `.remove()` call will grab `PciInfo` for us
device.remove(None, DetachGpuState::Remove, PcieLinkState::ShutDown).0?;
// Different `Device` because `.remove()` consumes the `Device`
let pci_info = device2.pci_info()?;
// Pass in our own `PciInfo`, call will use it instead
device2.remove(pci_info, DetachGpuState::Remove, PcieLinkState::ShutDown).0?;
```

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

Waits on events for the given timeout (in ms) and delivers one when it arrives.

See the `high_level::event_loop` module for an abstracted version of this.

This method returns immediately if an event is ready to be delivered when it is called. If no events are ready it will sleep until an event arrives, but not longer than the specified timeout. In certain conditions, this method could return before the timeout passes (e.g. when an interrupt arrives).

In the case of an XID error, the function returns the most recent XID error type seen by the system. If there are multiple XID errors generated before this method is called, the last seen XID error type will be returned for all XID error events.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-1)Errors

- `Uninitialized`, if the library has not been successfully initialized
- `Timeout`, if no event arrived in the specified timeout or an interrupt arrived
- `GpuLost`, if a GPU has fallen off the bus or is otherwise inaccessible
- `Unknown`, on any unexpected error

[§](https://docs.rs#device-support)Device Support

Supports Fermi and newer fully supported devices.

# GpmSample in nvml_wrapper::gpm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/nvml-wrapper/0.12.1/nvml_wrapper/gpm/struct.GpmSample.html

`pub struct GpmSample<'nvml> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Handle to a GPM (GPU Performance Monitoring) sample.

GPM enables collecting fine-grained GPU performance metrics (SM occupancy,
tensor utilization, PCIe/NVLink bandwidth, etc.) on Hopper+ GPUs. Metrics
are computed by taking two time-separated samples and comparing them via
[ gpm_metrics_get](https://docs.rs/fn.gpm_metrics_get.html).

**Operations on a sample are not thread-safe.** It does not, therefore,
implement `Sync`.

You can obtain a `GpmSample` via [ crate::Device::gpm_sample()](https://docs.rs/device/struct.Device.html#method.gpm_sample) or

[.](https://docs.rs/device/struct.Device.html#method.gpm_mig_sample)

`crate::Device::gpm_mig_sample()`Lifetimes are used to enforce that each `GpmSample` instance cannot be used
after the `Nvml` instance it was obtained from is dropped.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Use this to free the sample if you care about handling potential errors
(*the  Drop implementation ignores errors!*).

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

- `Uninitialized`, if the library has not been successfully initialized
- `Unknown`, on any unexpected error

# NvLink in nvml_wrapper::nv_link - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/nvml-wrapper/0.12.1/nvml_wrapper/nv_link/struct.NvLink.html

`pub struct NvLink<'device, 'nvml: 'device> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Struct that represents a `Device`’s NvLink.

Obtain this via `Device.link_wrapper_for()`.

Lifetimes are used to enforce that each `NvLink` instance cannot be used after
the `Device` instance it was obtained from is dropped:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use nvml_wrapper::Nvml;
let nvml = Nvml::init()?;
let device = nvml.device_by_index(0)?;
let link = device.link_wrapper_for(0);
drop(device);
// This won't compile
link.is_active()?;
```
Note that I cannot test any `NvLink` methods myself as I do not have access to
such a link setup. **Test the functionality in this module before you use it**.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/nvml_wrapper/nv_link.rs.html#401-424)#### pub fn [utilization_counter](https://docs.rs#method.utilization_counter)(
    &self,
    counter: [Counter](https://docs.rs/enums/nv_link/enum.Counter.html),
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[UtilizationCounter](https://docs.rs/structs/nv_link/struct.UtilizationCounter.html), [NvmlError](https://docs.rs/error/enum.NvmlError.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/nvml_wrapper/nv_link.rs.html#401-424)

#### pub fn [utilization_counter](https://docs.rs#method.utilization_counter)(
    &self,
    counter: [Counter](https://docs.rs/enums/nv_link/enum.Counter.html),
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[UtilizationCounter](https://docs.rs/structs/nv_link/struct.UtilizationCounter.html), [NvmlError](https://docs.rs/error/enum.NvmlError.html)>

Gets the NvLink utilization counter for the given `counter`.

The retrieved values are based on the current controls set for the specified
`Counter`. **You should use  .set_utilization_control() before calling this**
as the utilization counters have no default state.

I do not attempt to verify, statically or at runtime, that you have controls
set for `counter` prior to calling this method on `counter`. NVIDIA says that
it is “In general[,] good practice”, which does not sound to me as if it
is in any way unsafe to make this call without having set controls. I don’t
believe it’s worth the overhead of using a `Mutex`’d bool to track whether
or not you have set controls, and it’s certainly not worth the effort to
statically verify it via the type system.

That being said, I don’t know what exactly would happen, either, and I have no means of finding out. If you do and discover that garbage values are returned, for instance, I would love to hear about it; that would likely cause this decision to be reconsidered.

# Unit in nvml_wrapper::unit - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/nvml-wrapper/0.12.1/nvml_wrapper/unit/struct.Unit.html

`pub struct Unit<'nvml> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Struct that represents a unit.

Obtain a `Unit` with the various methods available to you on the `Nvml`
struct.

Lifetimes are used to enforce that each `Unit` instance cannot be used after
the `Nvml` instance it was obtained from is dropped:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use nvml_wrapper::Nvml;
let nvml = Nvml::init()?;
let unit = nvml.unit_by_index(0)?;
drop(nvml);
// This won't compile
let unit_devices = unit.devices()?;
```
Note that I cannot test any `Unit` methods myself as I do not have access to
such hardware. **Test the functionality in this module before you use it**.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

# Nvml in nvml_wrapper - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/nvml-wrapper/0.12.1/nvml_wrapper/struct.Nvml.html

`pub struct Nvml { /* private fields */ }`## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Handles NVML initialization and must be called before doing anything else.

While it is possible to initialize `NVML` multiple times (NVIDIA’s docs state
that reference counting is used internally), you should strive to initialize
`NVML` once at the start of your program’s execution; the constructors handle
dynamically loading function symbols from the `NVML` lib and are therefore
somewhat expensive.

Note that this will initialize NVML but not any GPUs. This means that NVML can communicate with a GPU even when other GPUs in a system are bad or unstable.

By default, initialization looks for “libnvidia-ml.so” on linux and “nvml.dll”
on Windows. These default names should work for default installs on those
platforms; if further specification is required, use `Nvml::builder`.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

- `DriverNotLoaded`, if the NVIDIA driver is not running
- `NoPermission`, if NVML does not have permission to talk to the driver
- `Unknown`, on any unexpected error

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/nvml_wrapper/lib.rs.html#335-337)#### pub fn [init_with_flags](https://docs.rs#method.init_with_flags)(flags: [InitFlags](https://docs.rs/bitmasks/struct.InitFlags.html)) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self, [NvmlError](https://docs.rs/error/enum.NvmlError.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/nvml_wrapper/lib.rs.html#335-337)

#### pub fn [init_with_flags](https://docs.rs#method.init_with_flags)(flags: [InitFlags](https://docs.rs/bitmasks/struct.InitFlags.html)) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self, [NvmlError](https://docs.rs/error/enum.NvmlError.html)>

An initialization function that allows you to pass flags to control certain behaviors.

This is the same as `init()` except for the addition of flags.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-1)Errors

- `DriverNotLoaded`, if the NVIDIA driver is not running

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-7)Errors

- `Uninitialized`, if the library has not been successfully initialized
- `InvalidArg`, if the length is 0 (if this is returned without length being 0, file an issue)
- `NotFound`, if the process does not exist
- `NoPermission`, if the user doesn’t have permission to perform the operation
- `Utf8Error`, if the string obtained from the C function is not valid UTF-8. NVIDIA’s docs say that the string encoding is ANSI, so this may very well happen.
- `Unknown`, on any unexpected error

Acquire the handle for a particular device based on its index (starts at 0).

Usage of this function causes NVML to initialize the target GPU. Additional GPUs may be initialized if the target GPU is an SLI slave.

You can determine valid indices by using `.device_count()`. This
function doesn’t call that for you, but the actual C function to get
the device handle will return an error in the case of an invalid index.
This means that the `InvalidArg` error will be returned if you pass in
an invalid index.

NVIDIA’s docs state that “The order in which NVML enumerates devices has
no guarantees of consistency between reboots. For that reason it is recommended
that devices be looked up by their PCI ids or UUID.” In this library, that translates
into usage of `.device_by_uuid()` and `.device_by_pci_bus_id()`.

The NVML index may not correlate with other APIs such as the CUDA device index.

- `InvalidArg`, if index is invalid
- `InsufficientPower`, if any attached devices have improperly attached external power cables
- `NoPermission`, if the user doesn’t have permission to talk to this device
- `IrqIssue`, if the NVIDIA kernel detected an interrupt issue with the attached GPUs
- `GpuLost`, if the target GPU has fallen off the bus or is otherwise inaccessible
- `Unknown`, on any unexpected error

Acquire the handle for a particular `Unit` based on its index.

Valid indices are derived from the count returned by `.unit_count()`.
For example, if `unit_count` is 2 the valid indices are 0 and 1, corresponding
to UNIT 0 and UNIT 1.

Note that the order in which NVML enumerates units has no guarantees of consistency between reboots.

Request the OS and the NVIDIA kernel driver to rediscover a portion of the PCI subsystem in search of GPUs that were previously removed.

The portion of the PCI tree can be narrowed by specifying a domain, bus, and
device in the passed-in `pci_info`. **If all of these fields are zeroes, the
entire PCI tree will be searched.** Note that for long-running NVML processes,
the enumeration of devices will change based on how many GPUs are discovered
and where they are inserted in bus order.

All newly discovered GPUs will be initialized and have their ECC scrubbed which
may take several seconds per GPU. **All device handles are no longer guaranteed
to be valid post discovery**. I am not sure if this means **all** device
handles, literally, or if NVIDIA is referring to handles that had previously
been obtained to devices that were then removed and have now been
re-discovered.

Must be run as administrator.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-19)Errors

- `Uninitialized`, if the library has not been successfully initialized
- `OperatingSystem`, if the operating system is denying this feature
- `NoPermission`, if the calling process has insufficient permissions to perform this operation
- `NulError`, if an issue is encountered when trying to convert a Rust- `String`into a- `CString`.
- `Unknown`, on any unexpected error

Some Kepler devices are also supported (that’s all NVIDIA says, no specifics).

# FieldIdScheme in nvml_wrapper - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/nvml-wrapper/0.12.1/nvml_wrapper/enum.FieldIdScheme.html

```
pub enum FieldIdScheme {
    V12,
    V13Update1,
}
```
## Expand description

The main struct that this library revolves around.

According to NVIDIA’s documentation, “It is the user’s responsibility to call `nvmlInit()`
before calling any other methods, and `nvmlShutdown()` once NVML is no longer being used.”
This struct is used to enforce those rules.

Also according to NVIDIA’s documentation, “NVML is thread-safe so it is safe to make
simultaneous NVML calls from multiple threads.” In the Rust world, this translates to `NVML`
being `Send` + `Sync`. You can `.clone()` an `Arc` wrapped `NVML` and enjoy using it on any thread.

NOTE: If you care about possible errors returned from `nvmlShutdown()`, use the `.shutdown()`
method on this struct. **The  Drop implementation ignores errors.**

When reading documentation on this struct and its members, remember that a lot of it,
especially in regards to errors returned, is copied from NVIDIA’s docs. While they can be found
online [here](http://docs.nvidia.com/deploy/nvml-api/index.html), the hosted docs sometimes outdated
and may not accurately reflect the version of NVML that this library is written for; beware. You
should ideally read the doc comments on an up-to-date NVML API header. Such a header can be
downloaded as part of the [CUDA toolkit](https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda-downloads).
Describes which field ID numbering scheme the loaded NVML driver uses for
IDs 251-273. NVIDIA broke ABI compatibility for these IDs between the
original CUDA 13.0 release and CUDA 13.0 Update 1 (driver >= 580.82).

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.V12)

### V12

Used by drivers before 580.82 (CUDA 12.x and original CUDA 13.0). IDs 251-255 are CLOCKS_EVENT_REASON/POWER_SYNC, 256-273 are PWR_SMOOTHING.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.V13Update1)

### V13Update1

Used by drivers >= 580.82 (CUDA 13.0 Update 1+). IDs 251-268 are PWR_SMOOTHING, 269-273 are CLOCKS_EVENT_REASON/POWER_SYNC.

# nvml_wrapper - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/nvml-wrapper/latest/aarch64-apple-darwin/nvml_wrapper/

## Expand description

A safe and ergonomic Rust wrapper for the [NVIDIA Management Library](https://developer.nvidia.com/nvidia-management-library-nvml) (NVML),
a C-based programmatic interface for monitoring and managing various states within
NVIDIA GPUs.

```
use nvml_wrapper::Nvml;
let nvml = Nvml::init()?;
// Get the first `Device` (GPU) in the system
let device = nvml.device_by_index(0)?;
let brand = device.brand()?; // GeForce on my system
let fan_speed = device.fan_speed(0)?; // Currently 17% on my system
let power_limit = device.enforced_power_limit()?; // 275k milliwatts on my system
let encoder_util = device.encoder_utilization()?; // Currently 0 on my system; Not encoding anything
let memory_info = device.memory_info()?; // Currently 1.63/6.37 GB used on my system
// ... and there's a whole lot more you can do. Most everything in NVML is wrapped and ready to go
```
NVML is intended to be a platform for building 3rd-party applications, and is also the underlying library for NVIDIA’s nvidia-smi tool.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

`nvml-wrapper` builds on top of generated bindings for NVML that make use of the
[ libloading](https://github.com/nagisa/rust_libloading) crate. This means the NVML library gets loaded upon
calling

`Nvml::init` and can return an error if NVML isn’t present, making it
possible to drop NVIDIA-related features in your code at runtime on systems that
don’t have relevant hardware.Successful execution of `Nvml::init` means:

- The NVML library was present on the system and able to be opened
- The function symbol to initialize NVML was loaded and called successfully
- An attempt has been made to load all other NVML function symbols

Every function you call thereafter will individually return an error if it couldn’t
be loaded from the NVML library during the `Nvml::init` call.

Note that it’s not advised to repeatedly call `Nvml::init` as the constructor
has to perform all the work of loading the function symbols from the library
each time it gets called. Instead, call `Nvml::init` once and store the resulting
`Nvml` instance somewhere to be accessed throughout the lifetime of your program
(perhaps in a [ once_cell](https://docs.rs/once_cell/latest/once_cell/sync/struct.Lazy.html)).

[§](https://docs.rs#nvml-support)NVML Support

This wrapper is being developed against and currently supports NVML version 11. Each new version of NVML is guaranteed to be backwards-compatible according to NVIDIA, so this wrapper should continue to work without issue regardless of NVML version bumps.

[§](https://docs.rs#legacy-functions)Legacy Functions

Sometimes there will be function-level API version bumps in new NVML releases. For example:

```
nvmlDeviceGetComputeRunningProcesses
nvmlDeviceGetComputeRunningProcesses_v2
nvmlDeviceGetComputeRunningProcesses_v3
```
The older versions of the functions will generally continue to work with the newer NVML releases; however, the newer function versions will not work with older NVML installs.

By default this wrapper only provides access to the newest function versions.
Enable the `legacy-functions` feature if you require the ability to call older
functions.

[§](https://docs.rs#msrv)MSRV

The Minimum Supported Rust Version is currently 1.51.0. I will not go out of my way to avoid bumping this.

[§](https://docs.rs#cargo-features)Cargo Features

The `serde` feature can be toggled on in order to `#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]`
for every NVML data structure.
